records.text: The confederation's archive says the conquest ended centuries ago. Your grandmother says it never quite ended. While correcting old tax records, you find a mountain town that has paid its dues for eighty years but appears on no map.

choices.text: Trace the town through the archive's payment records
Ask your grandmother what the old khipu say

ledger.text: The payments change from maize to copper to electricity, always under the same name: Qhapaq Pampa. A clerk warns you that the town was classified after a dam was built there. The paper trail is real, but someone has been carefully deciding who may read it.

choices.text: Make copies before the archive can close the record
File a formal request and force the archive to answer

khipu.text: Your grandmother lays knotted cords across the table. Their pattern names a settlement beside a river and records a promise of shared water. She cannot prove it is Qhapaq Pampa, but she recognizes the name as one used by people who refused to disappear into an imperial census.

choices.text: Carry the cords with you as testimony
Leave the fragile cords safe and travel with only their story

text.value: In Qhapaq Pampa, elders recognize the name your grandmother spoke. The dam lights their homes, but a company keeps the town's promised share of its power. Your archive has found a living community, not a historical footnote.

In Qhapaq Pampa, the old payment records match the town's own books. The dam lights their homes, but a company keeps the town's promised share of its power. Your archive has found a living community, not a historical footnote.

choices.text: Publish the evidence and let the country argue in daylight
Help the town negotiate quietly for its share
Stay and help the community organize its own archive

public_hearing.text: The records become public. The company contests every page, but the confederation's water council opens a hearing that cannot be hidden. The town wins no instant victory; it does win the right to make its case where everyone can hear it.

settlement.text: The company agrees to return part of the power revenue while the larger claim proceeds. Some villagers call it too little; others point to the school lights and clinic refrigerator. The dispute remains, now written in a contract the town helped shape.

living_archive.text: Children record the elders' accounts beside the engineers' maps and the old khipu. The town is still contested, but no longer absent. Your grandmother says that keeping a record is not the same as winning; it is how a people stays present for the next argument.
